candidates.title: The kinetoplastid kinetochore protein KKT23 acetyltransferase is a structural homolog of GCN5 that acetylates the histone H2A C-terminal tail
candidates.authors: Ludzia P, Ishii M, Deák G, Spanos C, Wilson M, Redfield C, Akiyoshi B.
candidates.abstract: SummaryThe kinetochore is the macromolecular protein machine that drives chromosome segregation in eukaryotes. In an evolutionarily divergent group of organisms called kinetoplastids, kinetochores are built using a unique set of proteins (KKT1–25 and KKIP1–12). KKT23 is a constitutively localized kinetochore protein containing a C-terminal acetyltransferase domain of unknown function. Here, using X-ray crystallography and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, we have determined the structure and dynamics of the KKT23 acetyl-transferase domain from Trypanosoma brucei and found that it is structurally similar to the GCN5 histone acetyltransferase domain. We find that KKT23 can acetylate the C-terminal tail of histone H2A and that knockdown of KKT23 results in decreased H2A acetylation levels in T. brucei. Finally, we have determined the crystal structure of the N-terminal region of KKT23 and shown that it interacts with KKT22. Our study provides important insights into the structure and function of the unique kinetochore acetyltransferase in trypanosomes.

candidates.title: Widespread Biosynthesis of Thiohistidine Dipeptides in Bacteria
candidates.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
candidates.authors: Abbott M, Leeman J, Kayrouz C, Ireland K, Davis K, Seyedsayamdost M.
candidates.abstract: Natural products have been paramount in inspiring novel chemistry as well as providing therapeutic agents and chemical tools for biological applications. A recently emerging class of natural products, the thio/seleno-imidazoles (TSIs), contains C–S or C–Se bonds that are installed by nonheme iron sulfoxide and selenoxide synthases (NHISSs). These TSIs, which include ergothioneine, are ubiquitous, but little is known about the broader TSI chemical space or co-occurrence with other biosynthetic enzymes. Here, we use NHISSs as a bioinformatic hook to identify a widespread family of biosynthetic gene clusters that encode a combination of NHISS and ATP-grasp enzymes. This search strategy enabled the discovery of two 2-thiohistidine-containing dipeptide natural products, one of which we isolated from the original microbial host. Structural and biochemical analyses of the corresponding biosynthetic enzymes revealed a novel NHISS active site architecture and an ATP-grasp enzyme with unprecedented substrate selectivity for 2-thiohistidine. Together, these results expand the known enzymology and distribution of TSIs and establish 2-thiohistidine as a biosynthetically encoded building block, enabling future discovery and functional investigation into this new natural product family.

candidates.title: ATP-driven dynamics and itraconazole binding of the drug efflux pump Cdr1 from Candida glabrata
candidates.authors: Pata J, Wiseman B, Zarkadas E, Baccouch R, Samrouth N, Desbois C, Moissonier L, Moreno A, Banerjee A, Aguerro S, Bettler E, Dujardin M, Magnard S, Terreux R, Schoehn G, Högbom M, Boumendjel A, Lamping E, Cannon RD, Prasad R, Chaptal V, Falson P
candidates.abstract: AbstractAzole resistance in Candida species is often caused by the overexpression of Cdr1. Despite its clinical relevance, the structural basis for its ATP-driven efflux pump function remains elusive. We present four high-resolution cryo-EM structures of Candida glabrata Cdr1 obtained in the absence and presence of ATP-Mg²⁺, itraconazole, and vanadate, capturing distinct nucleotide- and substrate-occupancy states. Additional low-population cryo-EM conformers were unveiled by 3D variability analysis, offering a detailed view of structural transitions linked with ATP-hydrolysis. The motion shows a 4 Å piston-like retraction of the C-helix from the γ-phosphate/vanadate of the hydrolyzed ATP. This causes the nearby transmembrane helix-1 (TMH-1) to open the drug-binding site via lateral displacement and unwinding of the inner-leaflet region of TMH-2. A reverse ‘squeeze-and-push’ motion of TMH-2 possibly drives substrate extrusion. High-resolution structures also reveal how itraconazole adapts its shape to fit into the drug-binding site. Our findings provide a dynamic structural framework for Cdr1-mediated azole resistance and the conserved chemo-mechanical cycle of ABC proteins, including non-membranous members.

candidates.title: Structural Snapshots of F1 ‐ATPase Catalysis in Drug Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Reveal Novel Therapeutic Targets
candidates.authors: Le K, Marzinek J, Mathiyazakan V, Bond P, Grüber G.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTGram‐negative Acinetobacter baumannii , one of the most critical priority pathogens, has developed multiple defense mechanisms, including upregulation of drug efflux pumps powered by the proton‐motive force (pmf) or ATP. As a nonfermenting bacterium, it relies on oxidative phosphorylation, in which the F‐ATP synthase, composed of an F1‐ATPase (α 3:β 3:γ:ε) and FO‐domain (a:b 2 :c 10), synthesizes ATP, the cell's currency of life. Here, we present cryo‐electron microscopy structures of the F1‐ATPase captured during ATP synthesis, revealing concerted conformational changes within the α 3:β 3‐catalytic head that trigger structural transitions of subunit ε and twisting of the γ:ε central stalk, coupled with spontaneous ATP formation. Molecular dynamics simulations validate and expand the ensemble of structural rearrangements underlying the rotary mechanism. The resolved intermediate states of the ε subunit reveal its role as a molecular gear, regulating ATP synthesis while simultaneously inhibiting ATP hydrolysis, essential for the pathogen to prevent wastage of ATP. These structural snapshots identify novel therapeutic targets and pave the way for rational design of selective inhibitors.Keywords: Acinetobacter baumannii , antibiotics, ATP synthase, bacterial pathogenesis, bioenergetics, membrane protein

candidates.title: TONSL/TONSOKU binding to histone H3.1 is required for DNA repair
candidates.authors: Davarinejad H, Laflamme C, Dupont B, Lunde-Ingrey S, Muñoz M, Joshi M, Sarvan S, Graham H, Ross A, Brunzelle J, Lavoie É, Alarcon E, Sheff J, Fradet-Turcotte A, Couture J.
candidates.abstract: AbstractIn plants, TONSOKU (TSK) regulates heterochromatic DNA replication and genome stability by preferentially binding histone H3.1 over its close homolog, histone H3.3. The structure of this interaction showed that a shallow pocket in TSK’s poly-tetratricopeptide repeat (TPRTSK) domain discriminates between the variants but did not report the importance of additional interactions underlying its binding to histone H3.1. In this study, we identify additional binding pockets that are important for histone H3.1 binding and TSK-like (TONSL)–dependent DNA repair. Consistently, sponastrime dysplasia-linked mutations in the TPR domain of TONSL impair histone H3.1 binding and fail to rescue TONSL’s DNA repair function in human cells. TPRTSK binding is highly regulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) on histone H3.1. Unexpectedly, TPRTSK contains two additional pockets that cooperate to recognize mono-methylated K4 and acetylated K27 on histone H3.1, two modifications associated with transcriptional regulatory elements like enhancers and promoters. Overall, our findings reveal that interactions between histone H3.1 and the TPR domains of TSK/TONSL are regulated by multiple PTMs and are functionally relevant for their DNA repair functions.

candidates.title: Network pharmacology–driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer’s disease
candidates.authors: Malakar V, Raman R, Justin A, SP D, Roy D, Malakar C, Purohit D, Mali P.
candidates.abstract: AbstractAlzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed for 128 active targets by STRING database and Cytoscape software. Further, active target-associated pathways analysed using ClueGO plugin Cytoscape software and the Reactome online public domain server. The non-competitive allosteric PTP1B inhibition through the design of Simufilam derivatives, with particular emphasis on A20, which is predicted to bind at the non-competitive allosteric site of the PTP1B protein (PDB ID: 1T49), involves α3, α6, and α7 helices that influence the WPD loop orientation. The proposed non-competitive allosteric binding mode is based on computational evidence and for that further experimental validation would be required to conclusively confirm binding of the designed compounds within this regulatory region. Using in-silico approaches, including molecular docking, identified A20 with the most favourable predicted binding energy score (−10.8 kcal/mol) compared to other derivatives. Molecular dynamics simulations further indicated structural stability of the PTP1B-A20, 26, and co-crystal complex, with consistent RMSD, RMSF, H-bond, Rg, and SASA. Principal component analysis suggested that A20 restricts conformational flexibility; hence MM-PBSA analysis displayed its stable binding free energies. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation characterized the polarity, stability, and reactivity of A20 studies supported its favourable electronic configuration. Overall, A20 displayed superior calculated binding energies, trajectory stability, and predicted drug-likeness, positioning it as a promising lead candidate for future empirical validation in AD research.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05086-2.Keywords: Simufilam derivatives, PTP1B inhibition, MD simulation 1000ns, MM/PBSA, DFT calculations

candidates.title: The MODNAP benchmark set for modeling ribose-based modified nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complexes: a case study with AlphaFold 3
candidates.abstract: AbstractModified nucleic acids play important roles in biology and biotechnology. However, their chemical and structural diversity as well as effects on nucleic acid structure and intermolecular interactions remain incompletely characterized. The performance of structure prediction and co-folding algorithms for modeling modified nucleic acids and nucleic acid–protein complexes has also not been evaluated. Here, we systematically analyze ribose-based modified nucleotides present in structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Modified nucleotides are primarily localized to the nucleobase, where they exhibit chemical and structural diversity shaped by molecular size, topological shape descriptors, and polarity-related properties. We develop MODNAP, the first curated dataset of experimentally determined structures containing modified nucleotides. Using MODNAP, we benchmark AlphaFold 3 on 1039 nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complex structures spanning a range of nucleotide modifications, tertiary folds, and biological functions. AlphaFold 3 achieves success rates exceeding 80% at an RMSD threshold of 2.5 Å. However, its accuracy in positioning modified nucleotides is variable and decreases for structures not explicitly represented in training. PoseBusters analysis reveals frequent intramolecular validity failures, primarily due to non-ideal ribose ring geometries. Together, these results establish MODNAP as a resource for evaluating and improving structure prediction methods for modified nucleic acids.

candidates.title: 7-O-sulfonation redirects luteolin’s target preference from furin to NS2B/NS3 and enhances anti-dengue activity
candidates.authors: Chen H, Lao Z, Huo Y, Yu L, Zhou W, Li G.
candidates.abstract: BackgroundDengue virus (DENV) infection remains a global health threat with no approved small-molecule antiviral for clinical use. Luteolin, a natural flavonoid, exhibits anti-dengue activity but suffers from poor solubility and moderate potency. The 7-O position is the primary site of metabolic glucuronidation, whereas the 5-O position is sequestered by intramolecular hydrogen bonding, offering structurally distinct positions for derivatization.MethodsFive site-selective derivatives of luteolin (three 5-O- and two 7-O-substituted) were synthesized. Their anti-DENV activity was evaluated in Vero cells by qRT-PCR (measuring viral RNA abundance) and plaque assays, and cytotoxicity was determined using the CCK8 method. For mechanistic exploration, enzymatic inhibition kinetics against NS2B/NS3 and furin were measured, and target engagement was further assessed via molecular docking and cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA).ResultsAmong the derivatives, compound 5, bearing a 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl group at the 7-O position, exhibited the most potent anti-DENV activity (EC50 = 0.46 μM) and the highest selectivity index (SI = 28.5), representing an 18-fold increase in antiviral potency over luteolin. In enzymatic assays, compound 5 showed preferential inhibition of the viral NS2B/NS3 protease (Ki = 11.54 μM) over the host furin (Ki = 93 μM). Molecular docking and thermal stabilization assays provided correlative evidence supporting target engagement with both proteases.ConclusionSite-selective 7-O-sulfonation of luteolin yields compound 5, a derivative with improved anti-DENV activity and selectivity that shows preferential NS2B/NS3 inhibition in enzymatic assays. This study provides a structural framework for the further optimization of flavonoid-based antiviral agents.

candidates.title: A phytochemical–nanotechnology platform exhibits complementary antimicrobial and immunomodulatory effects in experimental fowl typhoid
candidates.authors: Saleem A, Farhat B, Mir Y, Manzoor T, Nazir J, Ahmad S, Ganai A, Attia S, Prasad M, Ahmad S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractSalmonella gallinarum, the causative agent of fowl typhoid, poses a persistent threat to poultry health and productivity, compounded by the growing problem of antibiotic resistance. Addressing the urgent need for effective alternatives, this study evaluated a multi-component complementary approach combining the phytocompound 4-hydroxycoumarin, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), and Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) extract. In vitro assays, including antimicrobial susceptibility testing, cytotoxicity, and concentration optimization, confirmed the potent antibacterial activity and favorable safety profiles of the tested components. Molecular docking identified a putative interaction between 4-hydroxycoumarin and Chemokine (C-C motif) Ligand 5 (CCL5). Analysis of the archived molecular dynamics trajectory, after correction for periodic boundary conditions, revealed substantial protein conformational deviation and increasing ligand displacement toward the end of the trajectory, with a loss of close protein–ligand contact after approximately 40 ns. These findings support a predicted interaction but do not establish persistent ligand binding or a single predicted protein–ligand association mode. In the chicken infection model, the combination treatments were associated with descriptively reduced clinical severity and differences in endpoint mortality. These in vivo findings should be regarded as preliminary, descriptive, and exploratory proof-of-concept data, as mortality and clinical endpoint comparisons did not remain statistically significant after Holm correction. As 4-hydroxycoumarin was evaluated in vivo only as a component of the combination formulations, the observed effects belong strictly to the tested combinations, and their individual contributions cannot be determined independently. Gene expression analyses further revealed a downregulation of proinflammatory cytokines, providing exploratory evidence of immunomodulatory responses associated with the tested formulations. Together, these findings provide preliminary proof of concept for a multi-component approach against S. gallinarum infection.Keywords: 4-hydroxycoumarin, antimicrobial resistance, phytoremediation, poultry, Salmonella gallinarum

candidates.title: An inverse-protein-folding pre-trained model for predicting the mutational effects in protein-protein interactions
candidates.authors: Mao S, Meng S, Xiang Y.
candidates.abstract: SummaryProtein-protein interactions (PPIs) are fundamental to vast biological processes. Accurate prediction of mutation-induced changes in PPIs is crucial for protein engineering and drug discovery. Most existing PPI prediction approaches rely on refined physicochemical features or computationally intensive structural sampling. Here, we present delta-G message-passing-neural-network (DGMPNN), a message-passing neural-network framework for predicting the effects of mutations on PPIs. DGMPNN is pre-trained on an inverse protein folding (IPF) task and employs an adaptive residue-level attention pooling mechanism to enable effective transfer learning for predicting mutation-induced changes in protein binding affinity. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets and deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets. Experimental validation using computationally selected multi-site variants of the SARS-CoV-2 RBD-hACE2 complex showed strong agreement between predicted and experimentally measured binding affinities.

candidates.title: Angiotensin II exacerbates intracerebral hemorrhage in mice via heparin-like antithrombin activation and coagulation dysfunction
candidates.authors: Wang S, Xue M, Yan M, Liu C, Wang M, Yin Y, Yin Q, Lin S, Li W, Wang G, Lai R, Ni H, Tang X.
candidates.abstract: Hypertension has paradoxical prothrombotic-hemorrhagic predisposition toward cerebral infarction and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but the mechanism remains poorly understood. We observed Angiotensin II (Ang II) inhibited coagulation by activating antithrombin through heparin-like acceleration of antithrombin-thrombin interaction. Ang II allosterically modulates the 386-397 loop of antithrombin to enhance thrombin inhibition. In vivo, single injection of Ang II inhibited coagulation, alleviating thrombosis and aggravating ICH. Conversely, anti-Ang II monoclonal antibody promoted coagulation, aggravating thrombus formation and alleviating ICH. Notably, the blockage or deficiency of Ang II receptor had no significant effect on the alleviated thrombus formation or aggravated hemorrhage elicited by Ang II, suggesting the phenotypes were independent of Ang II receptor. In hypertensive mice, anti-Ang II monoclonal antibody significantly promoted coagulation and ameliorated ICH. These results identify Ang II as a key coagulation regulator with heparin-like function, suggesting that targeting Ang II-coagulation pathway could be a novel strategy to mitigate cerebral bleeding.

candidates.title: Bayesian Learning of Distance Metrics Beyond RMSD for Biomolecule Alignment, Clustering, and Domain Identification
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
candidates.authors: Mukherjee S, Hummer G.
candidates.abstract: AbstractRoot-mean-square deviation (RMSD) is the standard metric of structural comparison in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. In its conventional form, RMSD assigns equal weight to all atoms regardless of mobility. Hence, flexible loops and disordered regions can dominate a global RMSD, while the rigid functional core contributes negligibly to the overall metric. To address this issue, we introduce the Bayes-optimal RMSD (BRMSD), which optimizes per-atom weights jointly with structural averages by maximizing a Bayesian posterior. In a trade-off between low RMSD and weight uniformity, a position-fluctuation parameter σ controls the transition from classical RMSD (σ → ∞) to a progressive focus on a rigid core (σ → 0). The BRMSD framework supports analysis modules for structural alignment, focused alignment onto a user-specified domain, trajectory smoothing, soft K-means conformational clustering, and rigid-domain identification. These modules are implemented in the open-source Python package BRMSD and benchmarked on two MD systems, the endoplasmic reticulum translocon-associated protein SND3 and the phosphotransferase adenylate kinase.

candidates.title: Benchmarking Affinity-Based Docking for Irreversible Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors: A Physics-Informed Reactivity Framework for Stereoselective Potency Prioritization
candidates.authors: Kim J, Yoo J, Lee D, Kang K.
candidates.abstract: AbstractIrreversible organophosphorus inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) act by covalent phosphylation of the catalytic serine, yet their computational prioritization is often based on affinity scores from noncovalent docking. We benchmark that assumption against a curated set of measured human-AChE inhibition rate constants (n = 14; G-, V-, and organophosphate-pesticide classes, including a configuration-resolved VX pair). AutoDock Vina affinity (Spearman ρ = +0.12) and GNINA CNN scores (ρ = −0.40) do not provide statistically reliable potency rankings; explicit covalent docking also remains weak (ρ = +0.23, n = 11), with bootstrap confidence intervals crossing zero. Selecting covalent-compatible (near-attack) poses rather than top-ranked poses does not change this outcome. A quantum-chemical cluster scan supports a mechanistic interpretation: once the activated serine alkoxide/reactive complex is formed, P–O bond formation is downhill within the model, so the discriminating information is expected to reside in electrophilicity, leaving-group chemistry, and transport into reactive geometry rather than in a single docked pose. Consistently, mechanism-oriented molecular descriptors recover a modest but reproducible signal: TPSA alone correlates with potency (ρ = −0.62), and a Gaussian-process model used primarily for calibrated uncertainty yields leave-one-out ρ = +0.55 with permutation support (p ≈ 0.01) and a bootstrap CI whose lower bound lies near zero. A leave-both-VX-enantiomers-out test preserves the experimental S P > R P ordering. Given the small panel (n = 14), the descriptor correlations and stereochemical results are reported as exploratory and uncertainty-bounded rather than predictive. The resulting framework is presented as an uncertainty-bounded prioritization tool for data-scarce covalent AChE inhibitors, not as a substitute for kinetic measurement.

candidates.title: Cav3.1 Is a Neuronal Leucine Sensor That Mediates Satiety and Weight Loss in Response to Dietary Protein
candidates.authors: Tsang A, Heeley N, Alcaino C, Hwang E, Lam B, Rahman T, Darwish T, Nuzzaci D, Kay R, Sarkar A, Wang R, Basha N, Punnoose A, Kirwan P, Ma M, Merkle F, Gribble F, Reinmann F, Williams K, Blouet C.
candidates.abstract: SummaryDietary protein promotes satiety and weight loss but an understanding of appetite-regulating neurons sense dietary protein intake is lacking. Here we show that Cacna1g, encoding for the T-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav3.1, is enriched in hypothalamic leucine-sensing neurons and mediates neuronal leucine sensing. Pharmacological inhibition of Cav3.1 blunts leucine-induced activation of POMC neurons in cultured neurons and brain slices, as well as the anorectic response to hypothalamic leucine sensing in vivo. Genetic deletion of Cacna1g in POMC neurons abolishes the appetite- and weight-suppressive effects of high protein feeding. Mechanistically, we show that leucine binds to a hydrophobic pocket located between the voltage-sensing S4 segments of Domain II and III of Cav3.1, and thereby reduces its threshold for voltage-dependent activation. Last, we show that pharmacological activation of mediobasal hypothalamic Cav3.1 promotes weight loss in diet-induced obese mice and potentiates the weight loss response to anorectic agents such as liraglutide. Together, these results highlight the role of hypothalamic Cav3.1 as a neuronal leucine sensor and its relevance as a target for anti-obesity treatment.Keywords: Hypothalamus, Arcuate Nucleus, POMC neurons, Voltage-Gated Calcium Channel, Nutrient Sensing, Appetite, leucine, dietary proteins, Metabolic diseases, Obesity

candidates.title: Chemogenetic ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 CRISPR screen uncovers HAPSTR1/HUWE1 axis in chromatin proteostasis and cell cycle control
candidates.authors: van Overbeek N, Clijsters L, Wirth M, de Graaf I, de Lint K, Uruci S, Teunisse A, Akimov V, de Ru A, Vukic M, Kirdök I, Daxinger L, van Veelen P, Blagoev B, Luijsterburg M, Wolthuis R, Berlin I, Vertegaal A.
candidates.abstract: In this study, we sought to comprehensively map ubiquitin signaling networks at the crossroads of cellular proliferation and proteostasis, both crucial in cancer. Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening in the presence of the ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 identified 239 genes whose ablation sensitizes cells to ubiquitination blockade. Follow-up studies reveal a role for the nuclear protein, C16orf72/HECT, UBA, and WWE domain containing E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1 (HUWE1)–Associated Protein modifying Stress Responses (HAPSTR1), in chromatin proteostasis and DNA replication. We show that HAPSTR1 recruits the E3 ligase HUWE1 to the chromatin, keeping the chromatin-associated proteome in check, and is itself turned over by HUWE1 during cell cycle progression. Structural modeling of the HAPSTR1/HUWE1 complex, supported by mutational analysis, demonstrates that loss of HUWE1 binding renders HAPSTR1 unable to support cellular proliferation when ubiquitin signaling is suppressed. Consequently, HAPSTR1 ablation impairs clearance of chromatin-associated proteins, triggering global transcriptional and proteostatic adaptations. Under diminished ubiquitin signaling, these adaptive mechanisms give way to replication stress and premature S phase entry, culminating in cell cycle collapse and DNA damage. Our findings uncover protein networks exhibiting synthetic lethality with ubiquitin signaling blockade and highlight vulnerabilities of actively proliferating cells to proteostatic imbalance at the chromatin.

candidates.title: Comparative anthelmintic activity of artemisinin, dihydroartemisinin, and artesunate against sheep gastrointestinal nematodes: in vitro evaluation and exploratory β-tubulin molecular modeling
candidates.authors: Osmanlioglu Dag S, Alagoz M, Erez M, Kozan E, Ashraf S, Tatli Cankaya I.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundGastrointestinal nematode infections are an important constraint on small-ruminant production, and increasing anthelmintic resistance has intensified the search for alternative therapeutic compounds. Artemisinin and its derivatives have demonstrated activity against several helminth species, although comparative information regarding their effects on gastrointestinal nematodes remains limited. This study compared the in vitro anthelmintic activity of artemisinin (ART), dihydroartemisinin (DHA), and artesunate (ARTE) and explored β-tubulin as a candidate molecular target using complementary computational analyses.ResultsAll three compounds showed concentration-dependent activity against gastrointestinal nematode eggs and third-stage larvae. In the egg hatch assay, ARTE showed the lowest EC₅₀ value (63.45 µg/mL), followed by ART (82.02 µg/mL) and DHA (99.06 µg/mL). A similar activity pattern was observed for the predefined 24-h larval non-viability endpoint, with operational LC₅₀ values of 66.08 µg/mL for ARTE, 102.82 µg/mL for ART, and 185.41 µg/mL for DHA. Exploratory molecular docking against β-tubulin showed broadly comparable predicted binding at the colchicine-binding pocket, whereas ARTE exhibited the most favorable predicted interaction at the GTP-associated region. Molecular dynamics simulation supported the conformational stability of the predicted ARTE–β-tubulin complex over 150 ns, including persistent residue contacts and Mg²⁺ coordination. In silico ADMET profiling indicated distinct permeability and distribution characteristics among the three compounds without major structural toxicity alerts in the applied prediction tools.ConclusionsARTE showed the highest in vitro anthelmintic activity among the three evaluated artemisinin derivatives, with a consistent activity ranking of ARTE > ART > DHA in both experimental assays. The computational findings provide hypothesis-generating support for a potential interaction of ARTE with the GTP-associated region of β-tubulin but do not establish β-tubulin as its molecular target. Further parasite-specific target studies, in vivo efficacy experiments, pharmacokinetic evaluation, and direct target-engagement studies are required to clarify the biological mechanism and veterinary relevance of these findings.Keywords: Anthelmintic activity, Artesunate, Beta tubulin, Molecular docking, Molecular dynamics simulations, Nematodes

candidates.title: Comparative characterization and anti Helicobacter pylori activity of green synthesized silver nanoparticles from red and yellow fruited Ficus carica L. leaf extracts
candidates.authors: Al Jabri H, Nyamathulla S, Hashim N, Chung L, Farooq S, Naureen Z, Amri I, Halim S, Khan A, Hossain M, Al Harrasi A, Nthunya L, Al Hinai A, Al Jabri Z.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundGreen synthesis of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) using plant extracts offers an eco-friendly and sustainable approach for developing novel antimicrobial agents. Ficus carica L. leaf extract (FcLE), rich in bioactive phytochemicals, has potential as a natural reducing and stabilizing agent. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate AgNPs synthesized from yellow- and red-fruited F. carica L. leaf extracts and assess their antibacterial activity against Helicobacter pylori.ResultsFcLE exhibited strong bioreduction capability, likely mediated by the transformation of phytochemicals (catechin, myricetin, and epigallocatechin gallate) into oxidized derivatives acting as reducing and capping agents. Optimal synthesis conditions were identified at 1% (v/v), 50 °C, and neutral pH, ensuring nanoparticle stability and preventing agglomeration. Morphological characterization revealed distinct differences, with yellow-fruited FcLE producing monodisperse, spherical AgNPs (average diameter 3.87 nm) with a narrow size distribution, whereas red-fruited FcLE generated larger, clustered particles (~ 40–50 nm). X-ray diffraction confirmed a crystalline biphasic silver/silver oxide structure, with higher metallic silver phase purity (60%) in yellow-fruited FcLE-AgNPs. Zeta potential values (up to − 50 mV) indicated strong colloidal stability due to electrostatic repulsion. Antibacterial assays demonstrated moderate inhibition against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus (11 ± 0.6 mm and 10 ± 0.5 mm, respectively). Against H. pylori, yellow- and red-fruited FcLE-AgNPs produced mean inhibition zones of 20.00 ± 0.00 mm and 18.33 ± 0.58 mm, respectively, whereas the crude leaf extract showed no antibacterial activity under the tested conditions. Tetracycline produced a larger inhibition zone (49 mm) and served as the positive control. In silico docking further suggested that FcLE-derived compounds may interact with the urease enzyme.ConclusionsThese findings demonstrate that FcLE phytochemicals enable efficient synthesis of stable AgNPs at low concentrations and contribute to enhanced antibacterial activity. The synthesized nanoparticles exhibit promising In vitro antibacterial activity against H. pylori and warrant further investigation as plant-mediated nanomaterials for the management of H. pylori-associated gastric infections.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s11671-026-05009-3.Keywords: Red and yellow Ficus carica L., Silver nanoparticles, H. pylori, Molecular docking, Urease

candidates.authors: Nysten J, Van Eynde W, Lee Y, Vanhoffelen E, Desiderati G, Van Win T, Vande Velde G, Voet A, Robbins N, Cowen L, Van Dijck P.
candidates.abstract: The global rise in fungal infections, driven by expanding at-risk populations and growing antifungal resistance, highlights the need for new therapies. However, the current antifungal arsenal remains limited and emerging resistance reduces treatment efficacy. Through high-throughput screening of 20,000 drug-like compounds, we identified Z56812898, a benzamide linked to a bicyclic pyrimidine–pyran trione with novel antifungal activity. Guided by this hit, we discovered a structural analog with improved antifungal potency, Z247611722. This fungicidal compound has novel antifungal activity against multiple Candida species and fluconazole-resistant isolates. Chemogenomic, metabolomic, and phenotypic analyses revealed that Z247611722 disrupts sphingolipid biosynthesis by targeting serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT). The mode of action was confirmed by experimental evolution, yielding a resistant strain with a non-synonymous mutation in the SPT-encoding gene, LCB2. Structural modelling localized this alanine-to-proline substitution adjacent to the catalytic cavity, where it could alter the dynamics and conformation of the binding pocket and impair compound accommodation. Importantly, Z247611722 demonstrates in vivo efficacy in an invertebrate model of C. albicans infection. These findings validate SPT as a promising target and introduce a structurally distinct sphingolipid biosynthesis inhibitor with therapeutic potential.

candidates.authors: Sun W, Huang D, Long Y, Bao M, Xu Y, Wei H, Zhang G, Tao X.
candidates.abstract: Blueberry pomace is rich in bioactive compounds but limited by high moisture content. This study evaluated eight drying methods, including natural sunlight drying (ND-S), no-sunlight natural drying (ND-NS), hot-air drying at 45/160 °C (HAD45/HAD160), microwave drying (MD), vacuum freeze-drying (VFD), and combined steam explosion drying (SE-HAD and SE-VFD), for their effects on physicochemical properties, bioactive compounds, flavor, and inhibitory activity against α-glucosidase of blueberry pomace powder. Entropy analysis ranked SE-VFD as the highest in overall functional quality, followed by HAD45/VFD and SE-HAD. SE-VFD is promising for functional product development, whereas HAD45 may be a promising candidate for industrial production.

candidates.title: Computationally guided side chain optimization of nirmatrelvir for lead discovery against coronavirus main proteases
candidates.authors: Rahman M, Islam S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractTo optimize Nirmatrelvir as an inhibitor of the MERS-CoV main protease (Mpro), we developed an automated RDKit-based iterative scaffold optimization framework that integrated fragment replacement, combinatorial library enumeration, and chemical feasibility filtering to generate 15,744 drug-like analogs through systematic substitutions at six positions on the Nirmatrelvir scaffold. Structural similarity to Nirmatrelvir was assessed using complementary 2D fingerprint and 3D shape-based analyses of the 15,953 designed analogs and a separate set of 13,090 molecular weight-matched ChEMBL compounds to examine the binding potency in both the modified and randomly selected compound cohorts. Based on the correlation between structural similarity and docking score of the modified molecules, a binding score (BS) approach was advanced to rapidly identify and rank promising lead compounds. Several top candidates exhibited improved binding characteristics compared to that of Nirmatrelvir. To assess the robustness of the BS approach, multiple computational methods were employed, including KDEEP, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA) free energy calculations, and Boltz-2. The BS ranking showed strong agreement with all computational validation methods, consistently identifying compounds with enhanced binding affinities and stable protein-ligand interactions. The top-ranked compounds, M1, M3, M5, and M6, identified by high Binding Score (BS) values (9.1–10.2), exhibited favorable MM/GBSA binding free energies ranging from − 31.7 to − 42.9 kcal/mol, KDEEP-predicted binding affinities of − 9.5 to − 10.6 kcal/mol, and Boltz-2 predicted pIC₅₀ values of 10.0–11.8. Furthermore, for SARS-CoV-2 Mpro, BS scores also correlated well with available experimental half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) data and Boltz-2 predictions for Nirmatrelvir analogues. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the BS approach may serve as an efficient strategy for screening, prioritizing, and accelerating the discovery of next-generation coronavirus Mpro inhibitors.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s44345-026-00079-3.Keywords: MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro), Nirmatrelvir analogues, Molecular docking, Molecular dynamics (MD), MM/GBSA binding free energy, IC50

candidates.title: DEG2MOL: Conditional Latent Flow Matching for Transcriptome-Guided de novo Drug Design
candidates.authors: Kim S, Lim W, Lee H, Bong H, Kim J, Jeon M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractTranscriptomic profiles capture cellular responses to perturbations, offering a principled foundation for biologically grounded de novo drug design. However, existing transcriptome-guided generative approaches remain limited in biological specificity, transcriptomic coverage, and evaluation across diverse perturbation contexts. Here, we propose DEG2MOL, a biologically grounded conditioning framework that encodes differentially expressed gene profiles through a Gene Ontology (GO)-informed encoder and maps this representation into the latent space of a frozen, pre-trained scaffold-aware VAE via conditional latent flow matching. When benchmarked against five baseline models, DEG2MOL ranked first by rank-sum aggregation of six metrics in both the random- and scaffold-split evaluations. For two representative compound conditions, GO-informed encoder activations were accompanied by enrichment of the corresponding target-engaging pharmacophores among the generated molecules. In docking case studies of two compound–target pairs, generated molecules showed favorable predicted docking scores and reference-associated contacts. DEG2MOL also generated molecules from shRNA knockdown, CRISPR knockout, and Perturb-seq profiles without additional training, indicating transfer across the perturbation types and profiling platforms evaluated. At the transcriptional level, an in silico gene-expression analysis showed that the predicted signatures of generated molecules were more similar to those of target-matched inhibitors than to those of unrelated inhibitors. The data and code are available at https://github.com/KU-MedAI/DEG2MOL.

candidates.title: Designing Cooperative Molecular Glues for FKBP12-MAPRE1 with Enhanced-Sampling Molecular Dynamics Simulations
candidates.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
candidates.authors: Chen S, Solazzo R, Fouché M, Roth H, Dittrich B, Riniker S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractMolecular glues (MGs) offer a unique modality for inducing protein–protein interactions (PPIs), yet their rational design is often hindered by the limitations of static structural data. Here, we present a computational pipeline for the design of cooperative MGs for the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system using replica exchange with solute scaling (REST2) for enhanced sampling in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By sampling the conformational ensembles of binary and ternary complexes, we identified a “stabilized configurational space” that facilitates ternary-complex formation through a combination of conformational selection and induced-fit mechanisms. Based on the simulations, we developed a model that correlates PPI induction information from the simulations with the experimental cooperativity. This model was subsequently used to select and rank a small library of compounds prospectively, of which five were selected for synthesis and testing. Three of the five new compounds exhibited apparent cooperativity equal to or greater than that of the best previously known variants. This study demonstrates that targeting shared configurations within dynamic ensembles is a viable strategy for the rational optimization of cooperative molecular glues.

candidates.title: Domesticated bacterial origin genes regulate homeostasis of the insect gut microbiome and empower adaptation
candidates.authors: Zhang Z, Zhang Y, Zhao K, Cheng G, Lu Z, Wang D, Liu Y, Wu J, Wang L, Zhang L, Ye X, Yu L, Zhang W, Li Y.
candidates.abstract: AbstractSap‐sucking insects, represented by the globally distributed leafhoppers, have evolved a wide range of adaptive traits and play multiple ecological roles. However, their successful survival strategies in nature remain poorly understood. To explore the adaptive mechanisms of sap‐sucking insects, we established a research system using three representative leafhopper species from the same family and found that they have acquired multiple cholesterol‐dependent cytolysins (CDCs) derived from gram‐positive bacterial genes. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these CDCs have been domesticated and co‐evolved with leafhoppers, ultimately participating in various life activities of the host. Specifically, some CDCs exhibit high cytotoxicity, are specifically expressed in the egg serosa, and affect the feeding behaviors of leafhopper predators; others show non‐cytotoxic activity, are specifically expressed in the gut, and may regulate leafhopper growth and development by potentially maintaining the homeostasis of the leafhopper gut microbiome. It provides a comprehensive perspective to bridge the genotypes of acquired genes with the phenotypes of adaptive traits and demonstrates how homologous genes from donor organisms undergo functional differentiation in recipient hosts, enabling them to exploit new ecological niches. candidates.journal: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology

candidates.abstract: The Microprocessor complex, minimally composed of DROSHA and DGCR8, is ubiquitously required for microRNA biogenesis. It also regulates the balance between pluripotency and differentiation through mRNA alternative splicing and mRNA cleavage. However, how these various activities are regulated remains incompletely understood. Both DROSHA and DGCR8 are phosphoproteins, and phosphorylation has been reported to influence their molecular functions. In this study, we identified residues in DGCR8 by mass spectrometry that were differentially phosphorylated in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) before and after differentiation into neuronal cells. This included S95 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in undifferentiated cells, and S238 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in differentiated cells. By means of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing of the endogenous Dgcr8 gene, we generated a homozygous S95A mESC clone and a heterozygous S238A/- mESC clone. Both mutants retained an mESC phenotype but exhibited altered Microprocessor-dependent functions and differentiation outcomes. When directed toward the neuronal lineage, the S238A/- mutant displayed elevated mRNA expression of neuronal progenitor markers even after 10 days, while both S95A and S238A/- mutants failed to generate cardiomyocytes in embryoid body differentiation cultures. Furthermore, MEK1/2 inhibition with a highly selective inhibitor partially phenocopied the transcriptional effects of S95A in mESCs, consistent with a potential contribution of ERK/MAPK signaling for S95 phosphorylation. Together, these findings support a role for site-specific DGCR8 phosphorylation in modulating Microprocessor-dependent processes and differentiation in mESCs, establishing DGCR8 phosphorylation as an important regulatory mechanism in the regulation of Microprocessor activity, especially for stem cell differentiation.

candidates.title: Exploring the Molecular Mechanism of Ganoderic Acid B for Insomnia Based on Metabolomics, Network Pharmacology, Molecular Docking, and Experimental Validation
candidates.authors: Wan C, Du Y, Miu J, Chen P, Han Y, Sun S, Sun S, Wang L, Wang S, Bai H.
candidates.abstract: Objective: Ganoderma lucidum, a fungus of the genus Ganoderma in the family Polyporaceae, is often used in traditional medicine for the treatment of insomnia and amnesia, etc. Ganoderic acid B, a characteristic lanostane-type triterpenoid isolated from Ganoderma lucidum, has been preliminarily verified to possess mild sedative activity in existing studies. This study aims to explore the potential regulatory mechanism of Ganoderic acid B against PCPA-induced insomnia-like damage via multiple preclinical research strategies, and provide preliminary molecular and experimental clues for subsequent basic mechanistic research of this compound. Methods: Taking Ganoderic acid B as the research object, we established a PCPA-induced mouse insomnia model and evaluated its protective effects on insomnia-associated pathological lesions through behavioral assays, biochemical detection, and cerebral histopathological observation. Subsequently, UHPLC-MS/MS serum metabolomics analysis was performed to screen characteristic biomarkers and pivotal metabolic pathways linked to insomnia pathology. Next, compound and disease target databases were combined to obtain overlapping targets correlated with the alleviation of insomnia lesions by Ganoderic acid B; network pharmacology analyses, including GO and KEGG enrichment, were implemented to screen core hub targets, followed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation to preliminarily verify the binding interaction between Ganoderic acid B and these targets. Finally, an in vitro CORT-triggered HT22 neuronal injury model was adopted for experimental validation, and Western blot assays were conducted on mouse brain tissue to detect the expression of core regulatory proteins. Results: In vivo experiments showed Ganoderic acid B alleviated weight loss and abnormal behaviors, raised serum 5-HT and GABA, and lowered DA and NE in PCPA insomnia model mice. Metabolomics screened six key insomnia-related serum markers, with phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis as the core pathway. CCK-8 assays showed that 4 and 8 μM Ganoderic acid B had no cytotoxicity and relieved CORT-induced neuronal injury, while 16 μM inhibited HT22 cell viability. Network pharmacology identified six core regulatory proteins (EP300, HDAC1, ESR1, IL-6, TNF, NCoR1) mediating Ganoderic acid B’s protective effects against insomnia lesions, with Pathways in cancer enriched. Molecular docking verified stable binding between Ganoderic acid B and these targets. Western blot results indicated Ganoderic acid B downregulated NCoR1, EP300, HDAC1, IL-6, and TNF and upregulated ESR1 expression Conclusion: Ganoderic acid B alleviates PCPA-triggered behavioral abnormalities, neurotransmitter disturbance, and hippocampal neuronal injury in mice via multitarget, multipathway synergistic regulation of NCoR1, EP300, ESR1, HDAC1, IL-6, and TNF, and restores the disrupted phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthetic network. This work offers preliminary preclinical and molecular evidence to clarify how Ganoderic acid B relieves insomnia-related pathological injuries

candidates.title: Immune and inflammatory features associated with pyroptosis- and myocardial fibrosis-related genes in HFpEF: a machine learning study
candidates.authors: Gao B, Wang G, Xu Z, Peng M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractHeart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a heterogeneous syndrome marked by inflammation, immune dysregulation, and myocardial fibrosis. Whether pyroptosis intersects with fibrotic remodeling in HFpEF remains uncertain. Two murine cardiac transcriptomic datasets were integrated after batch correction and intersected with curated pyroptosis- and myocardial fibrosis-related gene sets. Functional enrichment, univariate logistic regression, support vector machine–recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were used for feature selection. Complete separation in the ordinary three-gene logistic fit prompted refitting with Firth bias-reduced logistic regression. Performance was assessed by apparent area under the curve (AUC), stratified bootstrap optimism correction, and repeated nested cross-validation; the panel was re-estimated in a human left-ventricular dataset for exploratory replication. Cell-type Identification by Estimating Relative Subsets of RNA Transcripts (CIBERSORT) estimated immune-cell fractions, and expression was examined in a high-fat diet (HFD)/Nω-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester hydrochloride (L-NAME) murine model and whole blood from patients with HFpEF. Six candidates—Pparg, Ace2, Smad2, Lcn2, Ptpn11, and Sqstm1—were identified. Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes analyses linked them to SMAD binding, autolysosome/amphisome activity, cellular senescence, efferocytosis, and renin-angiotensin signaling. In the 45-sample discovery cohort, the fixed Pparg-Ptpn11-Ace2 Firth model had an apparent AUC of 1.0000; bootstrap correction yielded an AUC of 0.9971 (95% percentile interval, 0.9780–1.0000). Repeated nested cross-validation produced a mean out-of-fold AUC of 0.9286 (2.5%–97.5% percentile interval, 0.8726–0.9700), revealing additional feature-selection uncertainty. Re-estimation in the human dataset represented panel-level replication rather than validation of a locked cross-species model. No inferred immune-cell fraction differed between HFpEF and control after false-discovery-rate correction, although exploratory correlations were observed among deconvolved fractions and with Ptpn11 expression. HFD/L-NAME-treated mice developed diastolic dysfunction, reduced exercise capacity, pulmonary congestion, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and myocardial fibrosis despite preserved systolic function; myocardial Ptpn11, Pparg, and Ace2 transcripts and their proteins were reduced. In patients with HFpEF, whole-blood PTPN11 mRNA was lower than in controls and inversely associated with N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide and C-reactive protein; these unadjusted findings remain exploratory. The three-gene panel is hypothesis-generating rather than a stable diagnostic model; its transportability, selection stability, and clinical relevance require prospective validation.Keywords: HFPEF, inflammation, machine learning, myocardial fibrosis, Ptpn11, pyroptosis

candidates.title: Improving ABFE Calculations for GPCRs by Addressing Errors in Apo-State Representation
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
candidates.authors: Anand N, Panescu A, Knegtel R, Chudyk E, Zuccotto F, Biggin P.
candidates.abstract: AbstractFree energy perturbation (FEP) methods provide a robust computational framework for predicting protein-ligand binding affinities and have seen increased adoption in drug discovery workflows. Among these, absolute binding free energy (ABFE) calculations are especially valuable as they enable affinity prediction for novel compounds without prior experimental data. However, their broader adoption is limited by setup complexity, sampling challenges, and variable performance across systems. These challenges are particularly pronounced in therapeutically relevant complex membrane protein systems such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). This underscores the need to evaluate ABFE performance in GPCR systems and to develop strategies to mitigate these errors. Here, we evaluate ABFE calculations across three GPCR systems: the adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR), the dopamine D3 receptor (D3R), and the metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5). We focus on three sources of systematic error in these systems: (i) inadequate resolvation of the binding pocket in apo-like alchemical states, (ii) inconsistent treatment of metal ions, and (iii) insufficient sampling of receptor conformational transitions between holo-like and apo-like ensembles. To address these issues, we introduce two methodological improvements: a biased grand-canonical-like water transport scheme to improve binding pocket resolvation, and a replica-exchange umbrella sampling (REUS)-based framework to quantify and correct the free energy associated with receptor relaxation to apo-like conformations. Together, these approaches reduce the systematic overestimation of binding affinities, improving agreement with experimental data while maintaining ranking performance. Overall, our results highlight the importance of accurately representing the apo state in ABFE calculations and provide a practical framework for applying high-accuracy free energy methods to membrane protein targets.

candidates.authors: Li H, Luo X, Cao Y, Jiang H, Guo Z, Zhu Y, Zhang L, Li Z, Li J, Wu H, Li P.
candidates.abstract: AbstractTraumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of severe disability, and its secondary injury remains a key focus of interventional research. Cannabidiol (CBD) has neuroprotective potential, but conventional systemic administration still has limitations. In this study, we fabricated an in situ-implantable cannabidiol-loaded gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) sponge (GM-CBD) with short-term cytocompatibility and hemocompatibility and no detectable in vivo abnormalities. Under a non-equivalent dosing regimen, GM-CBD and intraperitoneally injected CBD (10 mg/kg) showed distinct concentration–distribution profiles: in the GM-CBD group, CBD continuously accumulated in the perilesional cortex over 48 h, whereas serum CBD remained persistently low. GM-CBD concurrently upregulated tight junction proteins and CD31+ endothelial cell expression, downregulated GFAP⁺ astrocyte proliferation, and altered AQP4 distribution, thereby improving blood–brain barrier integrity and alleviating post-traumatic cerebral edema. candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundAbnormal mechanical load is a critical risk factor for intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), and nucleus pulposus (NP) cell senescence is a core pathogenic mechanism in IVDD. Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive ion channel, whereas the NF-κB pathway promotes cellular senescence. The classical formula Duhuo Jisheng decoction has shown potential benefits in IVDD-related conditions, and its core herbal pair Angelica Pubescens-Taxillus Chinensis accounting for its pivotal therapeutic effects.ObjectiveThis study aimed to identify the optimal concentration ratio of the Angelica Pubescens-Taxillus Chinensis component-based Chinese medicine (CBCM) for attenuating compression-induced NP cell senescence and elucidate its molecular mechanism.MethodsAn in vitro NP cell senescence model was established using 1.0 MPa compression. Subsequently, the effect of CBCM on senescence was evaluated using senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining, Western blotting of senescence-related proteins, and qRT-PCR analysis of senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors. Additionally, the impact of CBCM on the Piezo1 and NF-κB pathways was analyzed through Western blotting, qRT-PCR, and immunofluorescence double staining. candidates.abstract: Human serum albumin (HSA), the major transport protein in blood plasma, can substantially influence the distribution of therapeutic compounds. candidates.title: Oleanolic acid-derived triterpenoids with dual TGR5 agonistic and RORγ inverse agonistic activity
candidates.authors: Stamou P, Perhal A, Schwarz P, Hernández González J, Weal J, Chen Y, Skaltsounis A, Halabalaki M, Kirchmair J, Dirsch V, Kostakis I.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5) and the retinoid-related orphan receptor γ (RORγ) are key regulators of metabolic and immune pathways. This makes them attractive targets for developing anti-inflammatory and metabolic therapeutics. In this study, we designed and synthesised a series of oleanolic acid-derived triterpenoid derivatives to explore their potential as dual modulators of these receptors. The focus of the structural modifications was on the double bond, C-3 substitution, and A-ring rearrangements in order to investigate their impact on biological activity and establish structure–activity relationships within the pentacyclic triterpene scaffold. Biological evaluation using CRE–luciferase reporter assays identified oleanolic acid (1), oleanonic acid (5), and compounds 7 and 8 as TGR5 agonists with concentration-dependent activities. Oleanolic acid (1) and the newly identified seco-derivative 8 displayed the most favourable potency and efficacy profiles. Gal4–RORγ reporter assays demonstrated inverse agonistic activity for oleanolic acid (1) and compounds 7 and 8. Although 7 and 8 exhibited lower potency than 1, both retained pronounced inhibitory efficacy, indicating that substantial scaffold rearrangement remains compatible with RORγ modulation. A resazurin conversion assay showed no evidence of cytotoxicity under the conditions tested, supporting that the observed receptor effects were not attributable to general cytotoxicity. Molecular modelling and Nwat-MMGBSA calculations supported the experimental findings and emphasized the role of conserved buried water molecules in stabilising ligand–receptor interactions in both targets. Overall, these findings identify oleanolic acid-derived triterpenoids as promising scaffolds for dual TGR5/RORγ modulation and provide valuable insights for the future development of multitarget-directed ligands targeting inflammatory and metabolic disorders.

candidates.title: Peptide optimization to improve antigen presentation and antitumor responses in sarcoma
candidates.authors: Mauriello A, Ragone C, Cavalluzzo B, Tornesello A, Clemente O, Picozzi F, Gallo M, Tafuto S, Buonaguro L, Tagliamonte M.
candidates.abstract: Sarcomas are rare and heterogeneous malignancies for which therapeutic options remain limited, particularly in advanced disease. Standard treatments, including surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and approved targeted agents, provide marginal improvements in progression-free and overall survival, highlighting the need for immunotherapeutic strategies. Therapeutic cancer vaccines represent a promising strategy, but clinical efficacy has been limited by low antigen immunogenicity and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Enhancing antigen presentation and T-cell receptor (TCR) engagement through heteroclitic peptide engineering may overcome immune tolerance and improve vaccine efficacy. Preliminary data from our group demonstrate that heteroclitic peptides modified at TCR-facing and anchor residues enhance antigen-specific T-cell recognition, cross-reactivity with wild-type epitopes, and tumor control in preclinical models. In this study, we aim to design and validate optimized heteroclitic epitopes derived from sarcoma-associated TAAs. We developed an integrated computational and experimental workflow to identify and optimize HLA-A*02:01-restricted epitopes derived from sarcoma-associated TAAs. Candidate wild-type (WT) peptides were selected using NetMHCpan 4.1 based on predicted HLA binding affinity and subsequently engineered through systematic amino acid substitutions to generate heteroclitic variants. Optimized peptides were evaluated by structural modeling and molecular docking, followed by experimental in vitro validation using T2-cell HLA stabilization assays. Their immunogenicity was assessed ex vivo in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) isolated from HLA-A*02:01-positive sarcoma patients using IFN-γ ELISpot and peptide–HLA dextramer analyses. The sequential optimization strategy generated heteroclitic variants with markedly improved predicted HLA-A*02:01 binding for most target proteins. Structural modeling indicated preservation of the peptide backbone and TCR-accessible surface for the majority of selected variants. These predictions were supported experimentally: several heteroclitic peptides enhanced HLA-A*02:01 stabilization and prolonged peptide–MHC complex persistence in T2 cells. Ex vivo, optimized peptides induced stronger antigen-specific IFN-γ responses than their wild-type counterparts, with significant increases for SET, CAGE, PTPN1 and MAGE-A3, while multimer staining demonstrated recognition of heteroclitic peptide–HLA complexes by wild-type-primed CD8+ T cells. These findings establish a transferable workflow for engineering more immunogenic, yet antigenically faithful, HLA-A*02:01-restricted epitopes. Rational heteroclitic optimization may therefore provide a useful platform for the development of next-generation therapeutic vaccines for sarcoma and other tumors with low intrinsic immunogenicity.

candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTEvaluating Stachys hissarica extracts via DPPH, FRAP, and ABTS assays revealed that the aqueous methanolic fraction exhibited strong, ascorbic acid‐comparable antioxidant activity. HPLC‐PDA/ESI‐MS/MS analysis of the aqueous methanolic extract led to the tentative annotation of 35 metabolites, including hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives, flavonoid glycosides, acetylated and methoxylated flavones, consistent with the phytochemical profile of the Stachys genus. candidates.authors: Jin X, Yang S, Wang Q, Chen S, Wang Y, Yang Y.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBcl-2 is critical for tumour survival and serves as a promising anticancer drug target. Herein, a series of novel Bcl-2-targeted peptides were identified through structure-based virtual screening and systematic biological validation. Four candidate peptides were selected from the peptide library. MST results demonstrated that Peptide 1 exhibited the strongest apparent binding affinity towards Bcl-2 (Kd = 0.51 ± 0.03 μM), superior to VS-9 and other screened peptides. Molecular dynamics simulation, free energy landscape analysis, and MM/GBSA calculation further supported the predicted conformational features of the Bcl-2–Peptide-1 complex. MTT assays demonstrated that Peptide-1 markedly inhibited the proliferation of HT29 and Colo320HSR colorectal cancer cells, while showing limited effects on normal NCM460 cells. Bcl-2 knockdown attenuated the bioactivity of Peptide-1, and RT-qPCR and ELISA analyses revealed that Peptide-1 modulated Bax/Bcl-2 expression at both transcriptional and protein levels. Peptide-1 represents a promising Bcl-2-targeting peptide with antiproliferative activity against colorectal cancer cells.

candidates.title: Redox-state-dependent CO binding in MoFe nitrogenase: insights from EPR, IR, and QM/MM analysis
candidates.authors: Rana A, Joyce J, Mathe Z, Van Stappen C, Sengupta K, Lorent C, Zebger I, Decamps L, DeBeer S.
candidates.abstract: Nitrogenase drives biological nitrogen fixation through an eight-step cycle, in which “n” electrons and protons are accumulated across the En catalytic states. Carbon monoxide (CO), a noncompetitive inhibitor for Mo nitrogenase but a substrate for V- or Fe-only nitrogenases, has been widely used as a spectroscopic probe of nitrogenase's active site. Infrared (IR) spectroscopy reports on CO binding mode and coordination environments, while electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy characterizes CO-bound states via their non-integer spin states. Crystal structures reveal a µ2-bridging mode formed by substitution of a “belt” sulfide, suggesting that sulfide lability may be mechanistically relevant. However, the redox state at which CO binds and the assignment of the resulting non-integer spin states remain unresolved, obscuring their relationship to the N2 reduction cycle. Likewise, the mechanism and relevance of sulfide substitution remain unclear. Here, we combine static and stopped-flow IR, EPR spectroscopy, photolysis, and quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) calculations, supported by non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), to investigate CO binding under varying electron flux, varying CO pressure, and H2 pressure. We find that CO binds predominantly at the E1 state, whereas EPR-active species correspond to CO-bound E2 states. H2S is identified as the preferred leaving group, and the absence of hydrides supports a stable CO-bound state that is disconnected from the reductive steps of nitrogen fixation.

candidates.title: Sacubitrilat exerts potent antiarrhythmic effects through activation of natriuretic peptide receptor-C
candidates.abstract: AbstractIntroductionSacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor used in the treatment of heart failure, has been shown to exert direct antiarrhythmic effects on ventricular cardiomyocytes. However, the underlying mechanisms and molecular targets remain to be elucidated. This study, therefore, aimed at investigating the direct antiarrhythmic properties of sacubitril and exploring a potential involvement of natriuretic peptides in the context of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy (AIC).Methods and ResultsDiastolic sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ leak was induced in isolated murine ventricular cardiomyocytes by enhancing late sodium current with ATX-II, and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived ventricular cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CM) by 24-h tachyarrhythmic stimulation. Diastolic Ca2+ leak and Ca2+ transient kinetics were quantified using confocal and epifluorescence microscopy, while pharmacological tools (CNP, ANP, NPR-C agonist cANP4-23, and NPR-C blocker osteocrin) dissected receptor involvement. In silico modelling explored potential binding sites of sacubitrilat to NPR-C. CNP, but not ANP, reversed the increases in Ca2+ spark frequency induced by ATX-II in murine ventricular cardiomyocytes. This effect was reproduced by selective NPR-C activation with cANP4-23 and abolished by NPR-C blockade with osteocrin. In a similar manner, sacubitrilat suppressed pathological SR Ca2+ leak in both murine and human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes. This protection was fully lost when NPR-C was inhibited. Sacubitrilat did not cause any significant alterations in systolic Ca2+ release and SR Ca2+ load in murine ventricular cardiomyocytes. In silico modelling identified a plausible hydrophobic binding pocket for sacubitrilat at the NPR-C dimer, thus supporting a direct receptor interaction.ConclusionsThese data indicate that activation of NPR-C is both necessary and sufficient for the potent antiarrhythmic actions of sacubitrilat, mediating a selective reduction of arrhythmogenic SR Ca2+ leak in murine ventricular cardiomyocytes as well as in a cellular model of human AIC in iPSC-CM. NPR-C therefore emerges as a promising molecular target for the development of novel antiarrhythmic therapies suitable for patients with heart failure and arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.Keywords: Sacubitril, Entresto, Natriuretic peptides, NPR-C, Ventricular arrhythmias

candidates.title: Salidroside inhibits glioma cell migration and proliferation through CYP2E1-neuroglobin-cytochrome c mediated redox axis
candidates.authors: Panda L, Barhwal K, Kumar A, Biswal S, Tripathy D, Sable M, Sahu R, Chhabra G.
candidates.abstract: BackgroundGlioblastoma (GB) represents one of the most aggressive primary brain tumors characterized by poor prognosis, high relapse and resistance to conventional therapies. Salidroside, a naturally occurring glucoside derived from Rhodiola rosea, has been reported to exhibit pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative properties across multiple cancer models; however, its mechanistic basis in glioma and its therapeutic potential remain incompletely characterized.MethodsNeuroglobin (Ngb) protein expression was analyzed in 101 glioma brain tissue specimens and 5 normal brain tissues by western blot and immunohistochemical staining. In silico analyses of oxidized and reduced state of Ngb with salidroside was performed along with pharmacokinetics and toxicity predictions to computationally evaluate possible binding interactions and drug-like properties. Further, to determine the underlying mechanisms, in vitro assays were performed in U87MG and LN229 human glioblastoma cells treated with salidroside. MTT assay, transwell assay, Annexin V/PI staining, mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), CYP2E1 activity, intracellular NADPH levels, Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio and markers of oxidative stress including ROS assay and lipid peroxidation were also measured. The mechanism of Ngb aided apoptosis was investigated by protein expression of Ngb, caspase 3 and cytosolic cytochrome c in glioma cells.ResultsNgb expression in glioma tissues samples significantly downregulated with increasing tumour grade as determined by immunoreactivity and western blot analysis. In-silico analyses predicted a possible interaction of salidroside with reduced state of Ngb, In vitro studies suggested significant reduction in cell viability, migration and invasion in both U87MG and LN229 cells on supplementation with salidroside. These effects were accompanied by increased CYP2E1 activity, altered intracellular NADPH levels indicating induction of oxidative stress. Mitochondrial dysfunction, manifested as reduced MMP, elevated lipid peroxidation and increased cytosolic cytochrome c release indicated activation of intrinsic apoptotic pathway. Computational analyses additionally predicted a preferential interaction with the reduced form of Ngb, providing a mechanistic hypothesis warranting experimental validation.ConclusionSalidroside exerts multi-faceted anti-cancer effects in glioblastoma cells, potentially involving upregulation of Ngb levels in glioma cells, modulation of redox homeostasis, mitochondrial integrity and intrinsic apoptotic signaling.

candidates.title: Simultaneous activation and release of a microtubule inhibitor from amphiphilic polymeric nanoparticles
candidates.authors: Singh H, Thotakura A, Prakasham A, de Korver E, Palmans A.
candidates.abstract: Light addressable drug delivery systems offer opportunities to achieve spatiotemporal control over therapeutic activity while minimising off-target effects. Here we report the design, synthesis, and evaluation of a photocaged photostatin (proPST-1), in which the phenolic group of photostatin-1 (PST-1) was masked with an o-nitrobenzyl (ONB) photocage. Our strategy combines reversible photoswitching of the azobenzene unit with irreversible photolysis of the ONB group, affording active PST-1. Molecular docking studies suggested reduced predicted tubulin compatibility of proPST-1 due to the bulky ONB group relative to PST-1 thus silencing the dark state activity and enabling optical ON-switching. Encapsulation of proPST-1 within polymeric nanoparticles (PNs) formed from an amphiphilic polymer resulted in water soluble nanocarriers with high encapsulation efficiencies of proPST-1 (∼95%). Upon 365 nm irradiation, photolysis released the active cis-PST-1, weakening hydrophobic partitioning and promoting release from the nanoparticle core. In vitro tubulin polymerisation assays confirmed pronounced light-dependent inhibition, while cytotoxicity assays in cells validated concentration-dependent activity only after irradiation. This proof-of-concept study establishes a blueprint for integrating photocaging and photoswitching within nanocarriers to achieve dual activation and triggered release.

candidates.title: Split Cas12a Protospacer Engineering Enables Ultraspecific Recognition of a PAM-Less DNA Strand via an External PAM-Proximal Duplex
candidates.authors: Lamothe G, Veillette F, Iwe I, Corsano A, Shrestha S, Singh S, Bouchard C, Godbout K, Lu Y, Rousseau J, Pardee K, Tremblay J.
candidates.abstract: AbstractCRISPR-Cas12a is a programmable RNA-guided endonuclease whose activation by double-stranded DNA normally depends on the recognition of an adjacent protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM), which constrains target selection in diagnostic applications. Here, we divide the DNA activator into PAM-proximal (Pp) and PAM-distal (Pd) duplexes, spatially separating the PAM requirement from the interrogation of a PAM-less target sequence. FRET, electrophoretic mobility shift, fluorescence polarization, and functional assays indicate that either fragment can associate with Cas12a, but that robust productive activation requires the PAM-containing Pp duplex together with the Pd duplex. Our data further support a model in which PAM-mediated protein–DNA contacts stabilize an assembly-competent complex and facilitate binding of the PAM-less Pd target capture. Weakening hybridization between the guide and Pp with a chimeric DNA/RNA increased the dependence on PAM-mediated stabilization and improved structural selectivity in the Pp region and single-nucleotide specificity in the Pd region. The resulting split-duplex architecture provides an ultraspecific platform for resolving single-nucleotide polymorphisms in the PAM-less DNA strand.

candidates.title: Structure-based computational prioritization of Emodin-8-glucoside as a candidate ligand for the VEGFR1 kinase domain in the context of placenta previa
candidates.authors: Inan D, Karageçili S, Ali N.
candidates.abstract: AbstractPlacenta previa is a serious obstetric condition associated with abnormal placental implantation and hemorrhagic complications, for which no targeted pharmacological therapy is established. This study applied an integrated structure-based computational workflow to explore the intracellular VEGFR1 kinase domain as a candidate molecular target. Twenty-one phytochemicals were screened using AutoDock Vina and MOE, with Emodin-8-glucoside consistently prioritized among the highest-ranked compounds. Redocking of the co-crystallized ligand 8ST reproduced its experimental pose with a heavy-atom RMSD of 1.465 Å. Comparative 500 ns molecular dynamics simulations showed persistent binding-site association of Emodin-8-glucoside and the 8ST control. End-point energy estimates were method dependent, with MM-GBSA yielding a negative mean estimate while MM-PBSA yielded a near-zero estimate with substantial variability. DFT analysis produced a HOMO-LUMO gap of 0.13204 Hartree (approximately 3.59 eV). SwissADME and ProTox 3.0 identified low gastrointestinal absorption, P-glycoprotein substrate behavior, high polarity, and several predicted toxicity liabilities. Overall, Emodin-8-glucoside represents an in-silico-prioritized exploratory candidate requiring biochemical, selectivity, placental-cell, and pregnancy-safety validation.

candidates.authors: Huang M, Chen Z, Zhang R, Liu S, Xu D, Li B, Hu H.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTIn the present study, a series of curcumin analogs (A1–P3) were designed and synthesized for the inhibition of prostate cancer cells by targeting androgen receptor (AR). All synthesized compounds were structurally characterized by 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and high‐resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). In vitro cytotoxicity assays demonstrated that multiple compounds exhibited comparable or improved cytotoxicity against AR‐positive 22Rv1 cells as compared to dimethylcurcumin (DMC, ASC‐J9). Among these compounds, compounds A2, A3, B1–B3, D1, F1, F3, G1, G3, H1, and P3 possessed higher selectivity toward prostate cancer cells as compared to DMC. Compounds O1–O3, A1–A3, B1–B3, F1, F3, G1, I1, and P3 exhibited lower cytotoxicity against AR‐negative PC‐3 cells than those against 22Rv1 cells. Based on the cytotoxicity results, the structure–activity relationships were analyzed. In the AR protein suppression assay, compounds O1–O3, A1–A3, and I1 exhibited similar inhibitory effects on both full‐length AR (AR‐FL) and AR splice variant 7 (AR‐V7) as compared to DMC, while compound P3 exhibited significantly enhanced AR‐FL suppression effect as compared to DMC. In comparison, compounds B2, B3, F1, and F3 exhibited reduced AR‐FL and AR‐V7 suppression effects as compared to DMC; B1 and G1 exhibited no significant suppression effect on AR‐FL and AR‐V7, suggesting that these compounds might inhibit prostate cancer cells by multiple mechanisms. Molecular docking simulations further confirmed that compounds O1–O3, A1–A3, I1, and P3 displayed high targeting ability to AR. The probable binding modes of these compounds to AR were also revealed. By modifying the molecular structure of curcumin, this study identified several compounds (A2, A3, P3) with high inhibitory activity and selectivity against castration‐resistant prostate cancer cells by targeting AR‐FL and AR‐V7. These three compounds are promising new candidates for castration‐resistant prostate cancer drug discovery.

candidates.authors: Hwang B, Kim S, Song J, Kim H, Lee S, Moon S.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVESAngiogenesis is essential for tumor growth, tissue repair, and cell development. Rosa hybrida is a widely cultivated ornamental plant, and research on its petals has been conducted. However, despite the presence of flavonoids and terpenoids in the leaves, the biological activity of rose leaves remains unclear. This study investigated the anti-angiogenic potential of R. hybrida leaf extract (RLE) using a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-stimulated angiogenic model.MATERIALS/METHODSRLE was prepared, chemically profiled by high-performance liquid chromatography, and used in both in vitro and ex vivo assays. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were treated with RLE in the presence of VEGF. Assays for endothelial cell proliferation, tube formation, migration, invasion, and angiogenic signaling protein (VEGFR-2, protein kinase B [AKT], extracellular signal-regulated kinase [ERK], and endothelial nitric oxide synthase [eNOS]) phosphorylation were conducted. Molecular docking was performed to predict interactions between major RLE compounds and VEGFR-2. Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) level was also evaluated by immunoblot and gelatin zymography. The mouse aortic ring assay was used to assess microvessel sprouting.RESULTSRLE inhibited VEGF-induced proliferation, tube formation, migration, and invasion in HUVECs. RLE treatment also reduced the phosphorylation of VEGFR-2 and downstream signaling molecules, including AKT, ERK, and eNOS. Molecular docking supported the potential interaction between major RLE compounds and VEGFR-2. Additionally, RLE inhibited MMP-2-mediated extracellular matrix remodeling and attenuated VEGF-stimulated microvessel sprouting in the aortic ring assay.CONCLUSIONRLE exerts potent anti-angiogenic effects by modulating the VEGF/VEGFR-2 signaling cascade and inhibiting MMP-2 activity. As a previously underutilized botanical resource, RLE may serve as a promising complementary therapeutic agent for diseases related to angiogenesis.
